name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q01 - Fraction obtained as filtrate during chemical analysis

questiontext.text: When a living tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid and strained through cheesecloth, the filtrate obtained is technically referred to as the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Chemical Fractionation
Grinding a living tissue in trichloroacetic acid (\(\text{Cl}_3\text{CCOOH}\)) produces a thick slurry. Filtering this slurry through cheesecloth or cotton separates it into two distinct portions based on solubility.

Step 2: Identification of the Filtrate
The portion that passes through the filter cloth is the filtrate, which contains small biomolecules with molecular weights between 18 and 800 daltons. This fraction is technically termed the acid-soluble pool. The portion retained on the cloth is the retentate or acid-insoluble fraction.

Final Answer:
The filtrate obtained during chemical analysis is technically designated as the acid-soluble pool.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q02 - Most abundant chemical component in living organisms

questiontext.text: According to the average composition of cells, which of the following is the most abundant chemical compound in living organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cellular Composition Evaluation
Living cells are composed of water, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids, and inorganic ions. Evaluating their relative abundance based on percentage of total cellular mass reveals that water constitutes 70% to 90% of cellular mass.

Step 2: Comparison of Relative Biomolecule Abundances
Proteins constitute 10% to 15%, nucleic acids 5% to 7%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2%, and inorganic ions 1%. Therefore, water is by far the most abundant chemical compound in living organisms.

Final Answer:
Water is the most abundant chemical component of cells, accounting for 70% to 90% of total cellular mass.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q03 - Simplest amino acid having hydrogen R group

questiontext.text: In which of the following amino acids is the variable \(\text{R}\) group represented simply by a hydrogen atom?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Amino Acid Structure Principle
\(\alpha\)-amino acids possess a central \(\alpha\)-carbon bonded to four substituent groups: a hydrogen atom, an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a variable \(\text{R}\) side chain.

Step 2: Evaluation of Specific Side Chains
In glycine, the \(\text{R}\) group is a hydrogen atom (\(-\text{H}\)). In alanine, the \(\text{R}\) group is a methyl group (\(-\text{CH}_3\)). In serine, the \(\text{R}\) group is a hydroxymethyl group (\(-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)).

Final Answer:
Glycine is the simplest amino acid containing a hydrogen atom as its variable substituent group.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q04 - Total carbon count in palmitic acid molecule

questiontext.text: What is the total number of carbon atoms present in a molecule of palmitic acid, including the carboxyl carbon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fatty Acid Structure Analysis
A fatty acid consists of a carboxyl group attached to a hydrocarbon \(\text{R}\) group. Its general formula can be represented as \(\text{CH}_3\text{-(CH}_2)_n\text{-COOH}\).

Step 2: Carbon Count Determination
Palmitic acid has the chemical formula \(\text{CH}_3\text{-(CH}_2)_{14}\text{-COOH}\). Summing all carbon atoms yields 1 methyl carbon + 14 methylene carbons + 1 carboxyl carbon = 16 total carbon atoms.

Final Answer:
Palmitic acid contains exactly 16 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q05 - Most abundant protein found in animal world

questiontext.text: Which of the following proteins is the most abundant protein in the animal world?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Animal Protein Abundance
Proteins serve crucial structural and functional roles in living organisms. Among animals, structural fibrous proteins provide intercellular support and tensile strength.

Step 2: Identification of Abundant Structural Protein
Collagen forms the primary intercellular ground substance in connective tissues and is recognized as the most abundant protein in the animal world. RuBisCO, by contrast, is the most abundant protein in the entire biosphere.

Final Answer:
Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q06 - Most abundant protein in whole of biosphere

questiontext.text: Which of the following is the most abundant protein in the whole of the biosphere?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Biospheric Protein Distribution
Photosynthetic organisms across terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems utilize enzymes to fix carbon dioxide during the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis.

Step 2: Abundance Assessment
The photosynthetic enzyme ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO) is present in large amounts across all photosynthetic plants and algae, making it the most abundant protein in the entire biosphere.

Final Answer:
Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO) is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q07 - Monomeric unit comprising the cellulose polymer

questiontext.text: Cellulose is a homopolymer consisting entirely of which monosaccharide unit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Polysaccharide Polymer Nature
Polysaccharides are long polymeric chains formed by condensation of monosaccharides. A homopolymer consists of only a single type of repeating monomeric building block.

Step 2: Monomer Identification
Cellulose is a linear homopolymer composed exclusively of repeating glucose units linked together. Inulin, in contrast, is a polymer of fructose.

Final Answer:
Cellulose is a homopolysaccharide composed solely of glucose monosaccharide units.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q08 - Monomeric building block of the polymer inulin

questiontext.text: Inulin is a storage polysaccharide found in plants that is a polymer of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Inulin Classification
Inulin is a naturally occurring storage fructan carbohydrate found in many plants, especially in roots and tubers.

Step 2: Monomeric Composition
Inulin is a homopolymer composed of repeating units of the ketohexose sugar fructose, differentiating it from glucose polymers such as starch, glycogen, and cellulose.

Final Answer:
Inulin is a fructan polymer made up of fructose monomeric units.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q09 - Prosthetic group present in catalase and peroxidase

questiontext.text: In the enzymes peroxidase and catalase, which catalyse the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide, the prosthetic group is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Prosthetic Group
A prosthetic group is an organic cofactor that is tightly and permanently bound to the apoenzyme protein portion, participating directly in the active site.

Step 2: Catalase and Peroxidase Analysis
Both catalase and peroxidase catalyze the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen. In both of these enzymes, haem is the tightly bound iron-porphyrin prosthetic group.

Final Answer:
Haem is the prosthetic group of catalase and peroxidase enzymes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q10 - Essential vitamin constituent of NAD and NADP

questiontext.text: The essential chemical component found in the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and NADP is the vitamin:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Coenzyme Nature and Function
Coenzymes are organic molecules whose association with the apoenzyme is transient and often function as carriers of chemical groups or electrons.

Step 2: Vitamin Identification
Many coenzymes have vitamins as their essential functional components. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) contain the B-complex vitamin niacin (nicotinic acid).

Final Answer:
Niacin is the essential vitamin component present in NAD and NADP.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q11 - Relative abundance of elements in living tissues

questiontext.text: A comparison of elemental composition between earth's crust and a living human body reveals that living organisms contain a significantly higher relative abundance of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Comparative Elemental Analysis
When analyzing the earth's crust versus human body tissues, all major elements found in the earth's crust are also detectable in living tissues.

Step 2: Relative Abundance Evaluation
However, quantitative comparison shows that carbon accounts for 18.5% of human body weight versus 0.03% of the earth's crust, and hydrogen accounts for 9.5% versus 0.14%. Silicon is prominent in earth's crust (27.7%) but negligible in living tissue. Thus, living systems possess a distinctly elevated relative abundance of carbon and hydrogen.

Final Answer:
Carbon and hydrogen exhibit a much higher relative abundance in living tissues compared to non-living matter.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q12 - Inorganic constituents observed in acid soluble fraction

questiontext.text: During chemical analysis of living tissue, which of the following inorganic compounds or radicals are typically observed in the acid-soluble fraction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fractionation of Living Tissue
Grinding tissue in trichloroacetic acid separates soluble components from insoluble cellular polymers and structural debris.

Step 2: Distribution of Inorganic Ions
Inorganic ions and compounds such as sulphate (\(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\)), phosphate (\(\text{PO}_4^{3-}\)), sodium, potassium, and magnesium dissolve into the trichloroacetic acid extract and are thus detected in the acid-soluble fraction. True macromolecules remain in the acid-insoluble retentate.

Final Answer:
Phosphate and sulphate are representative inorganic constituents found dissolved in the acid-soluble fraction.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q13 - Substituent groups on alpha carbon of amino acids

questiontext.text: Amino acids are substituted methanes where the four valency positions of the \(\alpha\)-carbon are satisfied by which four groups?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Methane Substitution Principle
Methane has four covalent bonds directed towards the vertices of a tetrahedron. In \(\alpha\)-amino acids, all four hydrogens of methane are replaced by specific chemical substituents attached to the central \(\alpha\)-carbon.

Step 2: Identification of the Four Groups
The four substituent groups occupying these valency positions are: a hydrogen atom (\(-\text{H}\)), an acidic carboxyl group (\(-\text{COOH}\)), a basic amino group (\(-\text{NH}_2\)), and a variable side chain designated as the \(\text{R}\) group.

Final Answer:
The four valency positions on the alpha-carbon are occupied by hydrogen, a carboxyl group, an amino group, and a variable R group.

answer.text: Hydrogen, carboxyl group, amino group, and a variable R group
Hydrogen, keto group, hydroxyl group, and a methyl group
Amino group, aldehyde group, hydrogen, and an ester group
Phosphate group, carboxyl group, amino group, and a variable R group

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q14 - Classification of amino acids as acidic basic neutral

questiontext.text: Based on the relative number of amino and carboxyl groups, which of the following correctly pairs an amino acid with its chemical nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Criteria for Amino Acid Classification
An amino acid is acidic if it contains more carboxyl groups than amino groups, basic if it contains more amino groups than carboxyl groups, and neutral if it contains an equal number of amino and carboxyl groups.

Step 2: Evaluation of Selected Amino Acids
Glutamic acid contains two carboxyl groups and one amino group (acidic). Lysine possesses an extra amino group in its side chain (basic). Valine contains one amino and one carboxyl group with an aliphatic hydrocarbon side chain (neutral).

Final Answer:
Glutamic acid is acidic, lysine is basic, and valine is neutral.

answer.text: Glutamic acid - Basic, Lysine - Neutral, Valine - Acidic
Glutamic acid - Acidic, Lysine - Basic, Valine - Neutral
Lysine - Acidic, Valine - Basic, Glutamic acid - Neutral
Valine - Acidic, Glutamic acid - Basic, Lysine - Neutral

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q15 - Net electrical charge of zwitterionic amino acid

questiontext.text: At a specific pH known as the isoelectric point, an amino acid exists as a zwitterion. What is the net electrical charge of the amino acid in this zwitterionic form?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ionization Behavior of Amino Acids
The amino group (\(-\text{NH}_2\)) can accept a proton to form \(-\text{NH}_3^+\), while the carboxyl group (\(-\text{COOH}\)) can donate a proton to form \(-\text{COO}^-\).

Step 2: Net Charge Computation
In the zwitterionic dipolar state, the molecule simultaneously carries one positive charge on the protonated amino group (\(+1\)) and one negative charge on the deprotonated carboxyl group (\(-1\)). The net overall charge is \((+1) + (-1) = 0\).

Final Answer:
The net electrical charge of an amino acid in its zwitterionic form is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q16 - Carbon atom count in arachidonic acid molecule

questiontext.text: How many total carbon atoms are present in a molecule of arachidonic acid, including the carboxyl carbon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fatty Acid Length Comparison
Fatty acids are characterized by hydrocarbon chains terminating in a carboxylic acid group. Palmitic acid is a 16-carbon saturated fatty acid.

Step 2: Arachidonic Acid Carbon Enumeration
Arachidonic acid is a polyunsaturated fatty acid with an \(\text{R}\) group attached to a carboxyl group that totals exactly 20 carbon atoms when including the carboxyl carbon.

Final Answer:
Arachidonic acid contains exactly 20 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q17 - Physical difference between fats and oils

questiontext.text: Fats and oils are both glycerides containing fatty acids esterified with glycerol. Oils differ from fats physically because oils have:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Comparison of Fats and Oils
Both fats and oils are lipid esters of glycerol and fatty acids (monoglycerides, diglycerides, or triglycerides).

Step 2: Melting Point Relationship
Oils have lower melting points, primarily due to a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids with cis double bonds. Consequently, oils (such as gingelly oil) remain in a liquid state during cold conditions or winters, whereas fats have higher melting points and remain solid.

Final Answer:
Oils possess a lower melting point than fats and therefore remain liquid in winter.

answer.text: A lower melting point and remain liquid in winter
A higher melting point and solidify easily in winter
A higher boiling point and no double bonds
Complete water solubility due to numerous hydroxyl groups

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q18 - Structural identity and cellular location of lecithin

questiontext.text: Lecithin is an important biomolecule found in cell membranes. Chemically, lecithin is classified as a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Phospholipid Definition
Lipids containing phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic nitrogenous base are designated as phospholipids.

Step 2: Structure of Lecithin
Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) consists of glycerol esterified to two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group bonded to choline. It is an amphipathic lipid that forms the lipid bilayer matrix of cell membranes.

Final Answer:
Lecithin is chemically classified as a phospholipid.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q19 - Distinction between nitrogen base nucleoside and nucleotide

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets correctly represents a nitrogenous base, its corresponding nucleoside, and its corresponding nucleotide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definitions of Nucleic Acid Units
A nitrogenous base is a heterocyclic purine or pyrimidine ring. A nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous base attached to a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose). A nucleotide consists of a nucleoside esterified to a phosphate group.

Step 2: Evaluation of Nomenclature Hierarchy
For adenine: the heterocyclic base is Adenine; the base + sugar is Adenosine (nucleoside); the base + sugar + phosphate is Adenylic acid (nucleotide). In other series, uridine and cytidine are nucleosides, while uridylic acid and cytidylic acid are nucleotides.

Final Answer:
Adenine is the nitrogen base, adenosine is the nucleoside, and adenylic acid is the nucleotide.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q20 - Classification of abrin and ricin as secondary metabolites

questiontext.text: According to the classification of secondary metabolites, abrin and ricin belong to the category of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Secondary Metabolite Categories
Plants, fungi, and microbes synthesize secondary metabolites that are grouped into distinct categories such as alkaloids, terpenoids, essential oils, toxins, lectins, and drugs.

Step 2: Identification of Abrin and Ricin
Abrin (from Abrus precatorius) and ricin (from Ricinus communis) are highly potent plant-derived biological toxins. Morphine and codeine are alkaloids, concanavalin A is a lectin, and vinblastin and curcumin are drugs.

Final Answer:
Abrin and ricin are categorized as toxins among secondary metabolites.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q21 - Secondary metabolite category for concanavalin A

questiontext.text: Concanavalin A is a secondary metabolite classified under which category?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Lectins
Lectins are carbohydrate-binding proteins of non-immune origin found abundantly in plant seeds.

Step 2: Metabolite Categorization
In the classification of secondary metabolites, Concanavalin A is specifically identified as a lectin. Lemon grass oil is an essential oil, morphine is an alkaloid, and rubber and cellulose are polymeric substances.

Final Answer:
Concanavalin A is classified under the secondary metabolite group called lectins.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q22 - Secondary metabolites classified under the drug category

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of secondary metabolites are classified as drugs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Secondary Metabolites
Secondary metabolites encompass various chemical families utilized in pharmacology and medicine.

Step 2: Pairing of Drug Metabolites
Vinblastin (an anticancer agent) and curcumin (from turmeric) are categorized specifically as drugs. Morphine and codeine are alkaloids; carotenoids and anthocyanins are pigments; abrin and ricin are toxins.

Final Answer:
Vinblastin and curcumin are secondary metabolites classified as drugs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q23 - Reason lipids appear in acid insoluble fraction

questiontext.text: Lipids have molecular weights that do not exceed 800 Da, yet they are recovered in the acid-insoluble fraction during tissue analysis because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Lipid Molecular Weight
Lipids are small molecules with molecular weights typically ranging from 200 to 800 Da, which places them strictly in the micromolecular category.

Step 2: Mechanism of Insoluble Fraction Retention
In living cells, lipids are organized into lipid bilayers within cell membranes and organellar membranes. Mechanical disruption during homogenization shears these membranes into vesicles that are insoluble in aqueous acid. These vesicles cannot pass through the filter cloth and are retained in the retentate.

Final Answer:
Membrane lipids form water-insoluble vesicles upon homogenization and separate with the acid-insoluble retentate.

answer.text: They polymerize spontaneously into giant macromolecular covalent lattices
They carry high electrical charges that precipitate in trichloroacetic acid
They are components of cell membranes that fragment into water-insoluble vesicles
They are tightly covalently cross-linked to cellulose fibres during filtration

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q24 - Order of abundance of cellular mass components

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the correct descending order of percentage of total cellular mass of the given components?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Listing Percentage Values
The cellular mass composition given in standard reference data is: Water = 70-90%, Proteins = 10-15%, Nucleic acids = 5-7%, Carbohydrates = 3%, Lipids = 2%, and Inorganic ions = 1%.

Step 2: Arranging in Descending Hierarchy
Comparing the percentage ranges yields: Water (70-90%) > Proteins (10-15%) > Nucleic acids (5-7%) > Carbohydrates (3%) > Lipids (2%) > Ions (1%).

Final Answer:
The descending order of cellular abundance is Water > Proteins > Nucleic acids > Carbohydrates > Lipids > Ions.

answer.text: Water > Carbohydrates > Proteins > Lipids > Nucleic acids > Ions
Proteins > Water > Nucleic acids > Lipids > Carbohydrates > Ions
Water > Proteins > Carbohydrates > Nucleic acids > Lipids > Ions
Water > Proteins > Nucleic acids > Carbohydrates > Lipids > Ions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q25 - Specific biological function of the protein GLUT4

questiontext.text: What is the primary physiological function of the protein GLUT-4 in human cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of GLUT-4
GLUT-4 stands for Glucose Transporter type 4, an insulin-regulated transport protein found primarily in adipose tissues and striated muscle.

Step 2: Functional Role Assignment
GLUT-4 facilitates the transport of glucose across the plasma membrane into cells. Collagen functions as an intercellular ground substance, insulin is the hormone, and sensory receptors mediate taste and smell.

Final Answer:
GLUT-4 enables the transport of glucose into cells across the plasma membrane.

answer.text: Serves as a sensory receptor for smell and taste
Acts as a hormone regulating blood sugar

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q26 - End characteristics of the branched glycogen polymer

questiontext.text: In a branched polysaccharide chain such as glycogen, which of the following statements correctly describes the terminal ends?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Polysaccharide Chain Polarity
A linear or branched polymer of glucose has directional polarity based on whether the anomeric carbon (carbon-1) is free or involved in a glycosidic linkage.

Step 2: Glycogen Terminal Assignments
In glycogen, the terminal residue with a free anomeric hemiacetal group (capable of reducing Fehling's or Benedict's reagent) lies at the right end, termed the reducing end. The opposite terminal residue at the left end is the non-reducing end.

Final Answer:
In glycogen, the right end is the reducing end and the left end is the non-reducing end.

answer.text: The right end is the non-reducing end and the left end is the reducing end
The right end is the reducing end and the left end is the non-reducing end
Both right and left ends are reducing ends
Both right and left ends are non-reducing ends

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q27 - Structural basis for iodine test in starch

questiontext.text: Starch gives a characteristic blue colour with iodine (\(\text{I}_2\)), whereas cellulose does not give this colour reaction because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conformation of Starch vs Cellulose
Starch contains amylose which adopts a regular helical secondary structure in aqueous solution. Cellulose consists of linear chains linked by \(\beta\)-1,4 glycosidic bonds forming rigid sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds without coiling into helices.

Step 2: Mechanism of Iodine Binding
The helical interior of amylose possesses the exact dimensions to accommodate molecular iodine (\(\text{I}_2\)), forming a blue-coloured inclusion complex. Because cellulose lacks these helical cavities, it cannot entrap \(\text{I}_2\) and shows no blue colour.

Final Answer:
Starch forms helical secondary structures capable of holding iodine molecules, whereas cellulose does not contain such helices.

answer.text: Starch is a heteropolymer while cellulose is a branched homopolymer
Cellulose has high nitrogen content that chemically reduces iodine to iodide
Starch forms helical secondary structures that trap iodine, whereas cellulose lacks complex helices
Starch is completely water-insoluble while cellulose dissolves rapidly

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q28 - Structural nature and composition of chitin polymer

questiontext.text: The complex polysaccharide chitin present in the exoskeletons of arthropods is primarily a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nature of Chitin
Chitin is a structural polysaccharide found in fungal cell walls and arthropod exoskeletons.

Step 2: Monomeric Composition
Chitin is composed of repeating amino-sugar derivatives, specifically N-acetylglucosamine, linked by \(\beta\)-glycosidic bonds. It is classified as a complex homopolysaccharide.

Final Answer:
Chitin is a homopolymer composed of repeating N-acetylglucosamine units.

answer.text: Branched heteropolymer of amino acids and fatty acids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q29 - Terminal naming in the primary structure of protein

questiontext.text: In the primary structure of a protein depicted as a linear chain, the first and last amino acids are respectively designated as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Protein Sequence Polarity
Polypeptides have a directional backbone synthesized from the amino-terminal end to the carboxyl-terminal end.

Step 2: Positional Representation
By convention, a protein chain is represented with the first amino acid carrying a free \(\alpha\)-amino group (N-terminal) on the left end and the last amino acid carrying a free \(\alpha\)-carboxyl group (C-terminal) on the right end.

Final Answer:
The first amino acid is the N-terminal residue on the left end, and the last is the C-terminal residue on the right end.

answer.text: N-terminal amino acid at the left end and C-terminal amino acid at the right end
C-terminal amino acid at the left end and N-terminal amino acid at the right end
N-terminal amino acid at the right end and C-terminal amino acid at the left end
R-terminal amino acid at both the left and right ends

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q30 - Subunit composition of adult human haemoglobin molecule

questiontext.text: Adult human haemoglobin (Hb) displays quaternary structure and is composed of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Quaternary Structure Concept
Quaternary structure describes how multiple folded polypeptide subunits assemble together into a functional multimeric protein complex.

Step 2: Composition of Human Haemoglobin
Adult human haemoglobin (HbA) is a tetramer consisting of 4 polypeptide chains: two identical \(\alpha\)-type chains (each 141 amino acids) and two identical \(\beta\)-type chains (each 146 amino acids), forming an \(\alpha_2\beta_2\) complex.

Final Answer:
Adult human haemoglobin consists of two identical alpha subunits and two identical beta subunits.

answer.text: Two identical \(\alpha\) subunits and two identical \(\beta\) subunits
Two \(\alpha\) subunits, one \(\beta\) subunit, and one \(\gamma\) subunit

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q31 - Acceleration factor of carbonic anhydrase catalyzed reaction

questiontext.text: In the hydration of carbon dioxide to form carbonic acid (\(\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\)), carbonic anhydrase accelerates the reaction rate by approximately how many times compared to the uncatalysed rate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Uncatalyzed Rate Analysis
In the absence of any enzyme, the reaction between \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is very sluggish, producing about 200 molecules of \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\) per hour.

Step 2: Catalyzed Rate Calculation
With carbonic anhydrase in the cytoplasm, approximately 600,000 molecules of \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\) are synthesized per second. In one hour, this equals \(600{,}000 \times 3600 = 2.16 \times 10^9\) molecules. Dividing by 200 gives \(\frac{2.16 \times 10^9}{200} \approx 1.08 \times 10^7\), representing an acceleration of approximately 10 million times (\(10^7\)).

Final Answer:
Carbonic anhydrase accelerates the hydration rate of carbon dioxide by approximately 10 million times.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q32 - Rule of thumb for rate change with temperature

questiontext.text: For chemical and enzymatic reactions within a physiological range, a general rule of thumb is that the reaction rate doubles or decreases by half for every:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Temperature Coefficient Concept
The effect of temperature on the rate of chemical and biochemical reactions is described by the temperature coefficient (\(Q_{10}\)).

Step 2: Standard Rule of Thumb
As a general principle, within a sub-denaturing range, the reaction velocity doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature and halves for every 10°C fall in temperature.

Final Answer:
The rate of reaction doubles or decreases by half for every 10°C change in temperature in either direction.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q33 - Classification of enzymes transferring groups between substrates

questiontext.text: Enzymes that catalyse the transfer of a chemical group \(\text{G}\) (other than hydrogen) between a pair of substrates \(\text{S}\) and \(\text{S}'\) belong to the class:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Enzyme Classification System
Enzymes are systematically divided into six major classes based on the reaction type they catalyze: Class 1 Oxidoreductases, Class 2 Transferases, Class 3 Hydrolases, Class 4 Lyases, Class 5 Isomerases, and Class 6 Ligases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Class 2 Transferases
Enzymes that mediate \(\text{S-G} + \text{S}' \rightarrow \text{S} + \text{S}'\text{-G}\), transferring functional groups (such as amino, phosphate, or methyl groups) other than hydrogen, are Transferases.

Final Answer:
Enzymes catalysing the transfer of a group other than hydrogen are classified as Transferases.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q34 - Metal ion cofactor required by carboxypeptidase

questiontext.text: Which metal ion acts as an essential cofactor for the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Metal Ion Cofactor Mechanism
Metal ion cofactors form coordination bonds with active site amino acid side chains and coordinate with the substrate to facilitate catalysis.

Step 2: Carboxypeptidase Specificity
Carboxypeptidase is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that hydrolyzes terminal peptide bonds from the carboxyl terminus. The coordinated \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) ion polarizes the carbonyl group of the peptide bond.

Final Answer:
Zinc is the specific metal ion cofactor required by carboxypeptidase.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q35 - Criteria defining macromolecules versus acid insoluble lipids

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately characterizes true biomacromolecules and explains why lipids are recovered in the acid-insoluble fraction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Criteria for True Biomacromolecules
True biomacromolecules (proteins, polysaccharides, and nucleic acids) possess molecular weights in the range of ten thousand daltons and above and are formed by polymerization of repeating monomeric subunits.

Step 2: Behavior of Lipids during Homogenization
Lipids are small molecules whose molecular weights do not exceed 800 daltons and are not polymers. However, during mechanical tissue grinding, cell membranes and organellar membranes rupture and reassemble into water-insoluble vesicles that are retained on the filter cloth along with the macromolecular fraction.

Final Answer:
True macromolecules have molecular weights of 10,000 Da and above and are polymeric, while lipids (molecular weight under 800 Da) enter the acid-insoluble fraction because their membrane vesicles are water-insoluble.

answer.text: True macromolecules have molecular weights between 18 and 800 Da, whereas lipids form massive polymeric covalent networks exceeding 100,000 Da
Both lipids and true macromolecules are repeating homopolymers of fatty acids that precipitate upon acidification

True macromolecules have molecular weights of 10,000 Da and above and are polymeric, whereas lipids have molecular weights below 800 Da and appear in the insoluble pellet because cell membrane fragments form water-insoluble vesicles
True macromolecules dissolve in trichloroacetic acid due to their large size, whereas lipids remain completely insoluble

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q36 - Structural differences between purines and pyrimidines

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes heterocyclic purine and pyrimidine nitrogenous bases present in nucleic acids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Heterocyclic Rings
Nitrogenous bases found in DNA and RNA are classified into two structural types based on their skeletal heterocyclic rings: purines and pyrimidines.

Step 2: Ring Structure and Base Assignment
Purines possess a bicyclic structure composed of a six-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring; adenine and guanine are substituted purines. Pyrimidines consist of a monocyclic six-membered ring; cytosine, uracil, and thymine are substituted pyrimidines.

Final Answer:
Adenine and guanine are bicyclic purines, while cytosine, uracil, and thymine are monocyclic pyrimidines.

answer.text: Adenine and cytosine are substituted purines, while guanine and uracil are substituted pyrimidines
Thymine and uracil are double-ringed purines, whereas adenine and guanine are single-ringed pyrimidines
Purines have a single six-membered heterocyclic ring, while pyrimidines contain two fused rings
Adenine and guanine are double-ringed purines, whereas cytosine, uracil, and thymine are single-ringed pyrimidines

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q37 - Distinguishing levels of protein structural organization

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding the structural levels of proteins is accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Secondary Structure Characteristics
The secondary structure of proteins involves localized folding of the polypeptide backbone into regular periodic arrangements like \(\alpha\)-helices and \(\beta\)-pleated sheets. In natural proteins, only right-handed helices are observed.

Step 2: Tertiary and Quaternary Structure Roles
Tertiary structure represents the overall 3-dimensional folding of the polypeptide chain upon itself like a hollow woolen ball, bringing distant amino acid residues together to form active pockets; this 3D architecture is absolutely necessary for enzymatic and biological activities. Quaternary structure requires multiple polypeptide subunits.

Final Answer:
Only right-handed helices are observed in secondary structures of proteins, and tertiary structure is indispensable for biological activity.

answer.text: In proteins, only right-handed helices are observed in the secondary structure, and tertiary structure is absolutely necessary for biological activity
In proteins, both left-handed and right-handed helices are equally abundant in secondary structure
Primary structure represents three-dimensional folding stabilized by disulphide and hydrogen bonds
Quaternary structure refers exclusively to the conformation of single polypeptide chains folded into a hollow ball

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q38 - Energy relationships in enzyme activation energy curve

questiontext.text: In a potential energy versus progress of reaction diagram for an enzyme-catalysed reaction, the activation energy corresponds to the difference between:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Potential Energy Landscape
In any chemical conversion \(\text{S} \rightarrow \text{P}\), the substrate must absorb sufficient energy to reach a strained, high-energy transition state before bonds can break and re-form to yield product.

Step 2: Activation Energy Definition
Activation energy (\(E_a\)) is defined as the difference between the average energy level of the initial substrate \(\text{S}\) and the maximum peak energy level of the unstable transition state. Enzymes accelerate reactions by stabilizing this transition state, thereby reducing the activation energy barrier. The difference between \(\text{S}\) and \(\text{P}\) gives the overall reaction enthalpy (\(\Delta H\)).

Final Answer:
Activation energy is the energy difference between the average energy content of the substrate and the peak transition state.

answer.text: The potential energy of the substrate and the potential energy of the final product
The average energy content of the substrate and that of its transition state
The potential energy of the free enzyme and the enzyme-substrate complex
The potential energy of the transition state and the final product

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q39 - Chronological sequence of catalytic cycle of enzyme

questiontext.text: Which of the following outlines the correct chronological order of stages during an enzyme's catalytic cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stage 1: Substrate Binding
The catalytic cycle initiates when the substrate diffuses into and binds to the active site pocket of the enzyme.

Step 2: Stage 2: Induced Fit
The binding of the substrate induces a conformational shift in the enzyme protein, causing it to fit more tightly and snugly around the substrate.

Step 3: Stage 3: Catalytic Cleavage and Product Formation
The catalytic groups in the active site now lie in precise proximity to break chemical bonds in the substrate, producing the transient enzyme-product complex.

Step 4: Stage 4: Product Release and Turnover
The enzyme releases the finished reaction products from the cleft, regenerating the free active site to initiate another catalytic turnover.

Final Answer:
The sequence is: substrate binding, induced conformational change, bond cleavage forming the enzyme-product complex, and finally release of free products.

answer.text: Enzyme alters shape fitting tightly → Substrate binds to active site → Free enzyme releases products → Active site cleaves substrate bonds
Substrate binds to active site → Active site cleaves substrate bonds → Free enzyme releases products → Enzyme alters shape fitting tightly
Substrate binds to active site → Enzyme alters shape fitting tightly → Active site cleaves substrate bonds forming enzyme-product complex → Free enzyme releases products
Free enzyme releases products → Substrate binds to active site → Active site cleaves substrate bonds → Enzyme alters shape fitting tightly

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q40 - Competitive inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase by malonate

questiontext.text: In the classic example of competitive inhibition involving succinic dehydrogenase and malonate, which of the following statements correctly explains the mechanism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Resemblance and Competition
Malonate (\(\text{CH}_2(\text{COOH})_2\)) closely mimics the chemical structure of succinate (\((\text{CH}_2)_2(\text{COOH})_2\)), the natural substrate of succinic dehydrogenase.

Step 2: Mechanism of Inhibition and Reversibility
Because of this close steric resemblance, malonate competes directly with succinate for the substrate-binding active site of succinic dehydrogenase. The binding is reversible and mutually exclusive; increasing the concentration of succinate displaces malonate from the active site and restores maximum reaction velocity (\(V_{\text{max}}\)).

Final Answer:
Malonate acts as a competitive inhibitor by reversibly competing with succinate for the active site, which can be reversed by increasing succinate concentration.

answer.text: Malonate binds irreversibly to an allosteric site causing permanent denaturation of the enzyme
Malonate alters the primary amino acid sequence of succinic dehydrogenase
Malonate destroys the apoenzyme by covalently cleaving its peptide bonds
Malonate closely resembles succinate structurally, competes for the active site, and inhibition can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q41 - Distinguishing reaction catalyzed by class lyase enzymes

questiontext.text: Enzymes that catalyse the removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds, belong to which enzyme class?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Enzyme Reaction Mechanism Analysis
Consider the chemical transformation \(\text{X-C-C-Y} \rightarrow \text{X-Y} + \text{C=C}\). Here, groups \(\text{X}\) and \(\text{Y}\) are eliminated without the addition of water (non-hydrolytic cleavage), creating a double bond in the remaining carbon skeleton.

Step 2: Classification Assignment
Hydrolases cleave bonds by adding water. Ligases join two molecules using ATP. Isomerases catalyze intramolecular rearrangements. Lyases specifically catalyze the non-hydrolytic elimination of groups to generate double bonds.

Final Answer:
Enzymes that eliminate groups by non-hydrolytic mechanisms leaving double bonds are classified as Lyases.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q42 - Distinguishing cofactors into prosthetic groups and coenzymes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a prosthetic group from a co-enzyme?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cofactor Classification Principles
Enzymes requiring non-protein constituents consist of an inactive protein moiety (apoenzyme) combined with a cofactor to generate the active holoenzyme.

Step 2: Comparison of Prosthetic Groups vs Coenzymes
Both prosthetic groups and coenzymes are organic compounds. A prosthetic group is distinguished by being tightly and stably bound to the apoenzyme (e.g., haem in catalase). In contrast, a coenzyme's association with the apoenzyme is transient and occurs primarily during the course of the catalytic reaction (e.g., NAD/NADP).

Final Answer:
Prosthetic groups are tightly bound organic cofactors, whereas co-enzymes associate only transiently with the apoenzyme.

answer.text: A prosthetic group is always an inorganic metal ion, whereas a co-enzyme is an organic vitamin
A prosthetic group is an organic cofactor tightly bound to the apoenzyme, whereas a co-enzyme's association with the apoenzyme is only transient
A prosthetic group binds transiently during catalysis, whereas a co-enzyme is permanently covalently cross-linked
A prosthetic group is non-essential for catalytic activity, whereas a co-enzyme is mandatory

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q43 - Effect of extreme temperature on enzyme activity

questiontext.text: How do sub-optimal low temperatures and supra-optimal high temperatures differentially affect enzyme activity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Low Temperature Effect
At low temperatures, thermal kinetic energy is low, causing reduced molecular collisions between enzyme and substrate. The enzyme enters a state of temporary inactivation, but its covalent and non-covalent structural conformation remains intact and fully functional upon rewarming.

Step 2: High Temperature Effect
Excess heat imparts intense kinetic energy that disrupts fragile hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and hydrophobic interactions maintaining the specific tertiary structure. This irreversible unfolding denatures the protein, destroying the active site geometry permanently.

Final Answer:
Low temperature temporarily inactivates the enzyme without structural damage, while high temperature permanently denatures the enzyme.

answer.text: Both low and high temperatures irreversibly denature the tertiary structure of the enzyme
Low temperature denatures the enzyme, whereas high temperature preserves it in a temporarily inactive state
Low temperature preserves the enzyme in a temporarily inactive state, whereas high temperature destroys activity due to protein denaturation
Low temperature cleaves primary peptide bonds, whereas high temperature stabilizes hydrogen bonding

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q44 - Reason for reaction velocity plateau at Vmax

questiontext.text: As substrate concentration \([\text{S}]\) increases, the reaction velocity initially rises and eventually plateaus at a maximum velocity (\(V_{\text{max}}\)). Further increase in \([\text{S}]\) fails to increase velocity because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Kinetics of Substrate Binding
At low substrate concentrations, many enzyme active sites remain unoccupied, so increasing \([\text{S}]\) increases the rate of collision and formation of the ES complex.

Step 2: Enzyme Saturation Phenomenon
Because the total concentration of enzyme molecules in the system is finite and fixed, there comes a point where all active sites are continuously engaged in catalysis (100% saturation). Additional substrate molecules must wait until a product is released, establishing a maximum turnover limit (\(V_{\text{max}}\)).

Final Answer:
The velocity reaches a plateau at Vmax because enzyme molecules are fully saturated with substrate.

answer.text: The substrate molecules begin to competitively inhibit each other
High substrate concentration denatures the tertiary structure of the enzyme
The activation energy of the reaction rises continuously with substrate addition
All enzyme active sites become saturated, leaving no free enzyme molecules available

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q45 - Matching categories of various plant secondary metabolites

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs each secondary metabolite with its specific biological class?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of Nitrogenous Secondary Metabolites
Codeine is an alkaloid derived from the opium poppy Papaver somniferum.

Step 2: Analysis of Terpenoids, Lectins, and Pigments
Diterpenes (such as gibberellins and phytol derivatives) belong to terpenoids. Concanavalin A is a carbohydrate-binding plant protein classified as a lectin. Anthocyanin is a water-soluble flavonoid plant pigment responsible for red, purple, and blue coloration.

Final Answer:
Codeine is an alkaloid, diterpenes are terpenoids, concanavalin A is a lectin, and anthocyanin is a pigment.

answer.text: Codeine with Alkaloids, Diterpenes with Terpenoids, Concanavalin A with Lectins, and Anthocyanin with Pigments
Codeine with Terpenoids, Diterpenes with Alkaloids, Concanavalin A with Lectins, and Anthocyanin with Pigments
Codeine with Alkaloids, Diterpenes with Terpenoids, Concanavalin A with Pigments, and Anthocyanin with Lectins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q46 - Identification of aromatic amino acids group

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets contains only aromatic amino acids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Aromatic Amino Acid Definition
Aromatic amino acids possess side chains containing conjugated aromatic carbon rings (benzene or indole rings).

Step 2: Evaluation of Amino Acid Groups
Tyrosine (hydroxyphenyl ring), phenylalanine (phenyl ring), and tryptophan (indole ring) are the three aromatic amino acids occurring in proteins. Glutamic acid and aspartic acid are acidic; lysine is basic; alanine, valine, and leucine are neutral aliphatic amino acids.

Final Answer:
Tyrosine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan constitute the group of aromatic amino acids.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q47 - Comparison between inorganic catalysts and biological enzymes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly compares inorganic catalysts and enzyme catalysts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Operating Conditions of Inorganic Catalysts
Inorganic catalysts (such as platinum, nickel, or iron) are non-protein minerals that operate effectively under extreme industrial conditions of high temperature and high pressure without denaturation.

Step 2: Thermal Sensitivity of Enzymes
Biological enzymes are proteins whose delicate tertiary structure is vulnerable to heat denaturation, typically losing activity above 40°C. A notable exception includes enzymes isolated from thermophilic organisms living in hot vents or sulphur springs, which remain active up to 80°C-90°C.

Final Answer:
Inorganic catalysts function at high temperatures and pressures, while most enzymes are denatured above 40°C, except those from thermophiles.

answer.text: Enzymes are universally stable up to 100°C, whereas inorganic catalysts degrade above 40°C
Inorganic catalysts exhibit high substrate specificity due to tertiary protein folding, whereas enzymes lack specificity
Inorganic catalysts work efficiently at high temperatures and pressures, whereas most enzymes denature above 40°C, except those from thermophilic organisms
Both inorganic catalysts and biological enzymes permanently alter their chemical structure during the catalytic cycle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q48 - End products of glycolysis under diverse physiological conditions

questiontext.text: During the ten-step metabolic pathway of glycolysis, glucose is converted to pyruvic acid. Under varying physiological conditions and organisms, what metabolic end products are formed from this pathway?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Core Glycolytic Pathway
Glycolysis converts one molecule of glucose (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\)) into two molecules of pyruvic acid (\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_3\)) through ten successive enzyme-catalyzed reactions.

Step 2: Fate Under Anaerobic Conditions
In human skeletal muscle during intense anaerobic exercise, pyruvate is reduced to lactic acid. In yeast undergoing fermentation under anaerobic conditions, the pathway leads to decarboxylation and reduction forming ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Final Answer:
Anaerobic glycolysis yields lactic acid in human skeletal muscle and ethanol during fermentation in yeast.

answer.text: Ethanol in human skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions, and lactic acid in fermenting yeast
Pyruvic acid in fermenting yeast under anaerobic conditions, and glycogen in human muscle
Cellulose in human skeletal muscle, and starch in fermenting yeast
Lactic acid in fatigued human skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions, and ethanol in fermenting yeast
